To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CWI is no better than active recovery at reducing muscle soreness and that it may be detrimental to recovery from local and systemic inflammation.
CWI has no greater effect than active recovery (AR) on muscle soreness, muscle function and systemic inflammation in humans.
CWI is no greater than an active recovery upon local inflammatory cellular stress in healthy humans.
In summary, our research is concerned with
investigating the impact of CWI on the recovery of elite and sub-elite athletes.
the impact of cold-water immersion on the recovery of skeletal muscle, and the associated systemic inflammatory response.
the impact of a single bout of CWI (10°C for 10 minutes) upon local and systemic inflammation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CWI is not superior to active recovery (AR) in the recovery of skeletal muscle function, but that it is a viable alternative for those athletes unable to perform AR.
there are no benefits of CWI over active recovery (AR) on local or systemic inflammatory responses, and that CWI may actually be detrimental to recovery.
there is no evidence of benefit of CWI over active recovery (AR) on any measure of recovery, including performance and inflammatory biomarkers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

CWI is not superior to active recovery (AR) in the reduction of muscle damage markers, and that CWI is associated with a reduction in the rate of recovery of performance capacity, and a blunting of the acute hormonal response.
the use of CWI is no more beneficial than active recovery in the recovery of local and systemic inflammatory markers.

CWI is a safe, inexpensive and effective recovery modality for the majority of sports.
